title: The Query Complexity of Local Search in Rounds on General Graphs
claim: Neighborhoods in the structured grid change one coordinate, while in the general graph they change many, so queries must run in parallel rounds.
layout: Top two panels side by side, bottom round-execution strip; color-coded contrast
description: The figure has three parts. The top left shows a 2D grid of gray dots with light gray lines. A blue central node X connects to four black neighbors (up, down, left, right). Its blue caption reads 'Neighbor differs by 1 entry'. The top right shows a gray 3D ellipsoid. A red node X sits at the center of a star of eight black neighbors, with a dashed equator line. Its red caption reads 'Neighbor differs by n entries (a row)'. The blue versus red colors and the sparse versus dense neighborhoods are the main contrast. The bottom strip is titled 'Execution in Rounds:'. Two horizontal bars each have seven downward arrows for a batch of queries. They are labeled Round t and Round t+1, and a double arrow labeled 'Update' links them.
caption: Left: In the Grid graph, a neighbor of X differs from X in a single coordinate. Right: In the Matrix graph, a neighbor of X differs from X in multiple coordinates (specifically, an entire row). This dense connectivity results in a high-expansion graph, distinct from a grid. Bottom: To mitigate high probe latency, the algorithm queries batches in parallel.
abstract: We analyze the query complexity of finding a local minimum in $t$ rounds on general graphs. More precisely, given a graph $G = (V,E)$ and oracle access to an unknown function $f : V \to \mathbb{R}$, the goal is to find a local minimum--a vertex $v$ such that $f(v) \leq f(u)$ for all $(u,v) \in E$--using at most $t$ rounds of interaction with the oracle. The query complexity is well understood on grids, but much less is known beyond. This abstract problem captures many optimization tasks, such as finding a local minimum of a loss function during neural network training. For each graph with $n$ vertices, we prove a deterministic upper bound of $O(t n^{1/t} (sÎ)^{1-1/t})$, where $s$ is the separation number and $Î$ is the maximum degree of the graph. We complement this result with a randomized lower bound of $Î©(t n^{1/t}-t)$ that holds for any connected graph. We also find that parallel steepest descent with a warm start provides improved bounds for graphs with high separation number and bounded degree. To obtain our results, we utilized an advanced version of Gemini at various stages of our research. We discuss our experience in a methodology section.
